title: The data geometry of masking diffusion: Certified-optimal schedules via unmasking growth complexity

paper.title: The data geometry of masking diffusion: Certified-optimal schedules via unmasking growth complexity
paper.abstract:
Abstract We study masking diffusion for discrete sampling and introduce a
path-resolved measure of data geometry called the unmasking
growth complexity ( UGC ). Its local increments
directly control Kullback–Leibler (KL) discretization error, yielding
a unified analysis of Bernoulli-subset and fixed-cardinality unmasking
schemes. In log-reveal-odds coordinates, this structure yields
optimized single-block and multi-block schedules, and quantifies the
gains from adapting computational effort to data geometry. Crucially,
we show how UGC increments can be estimated from
samples via KL increments along coupled reveal trajectories. This
leads to certified-optimal samplers that achieve a prescribed
KL error with high probability and iteration complexity within a
constant factor of the corresponding oracle procedure. Collapsing the UGC path yields the aggregate UGC mass, which
connects to classical multivariate dependence measures, and complexity
measures from previous analyses of discrete diffusion. In the
fine-partition limit, the squared integral of the square-root UGC density determines the sharp leading-order
optimal Euler discretization error. Examples exhibit substantial
dimension-dependent gains over coarse schedules, including Ω ~ ​ ( d ) \widetilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{d}) improvements achievable with a constant
number of adaptively placed blocks.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The problem of sampling from a high-dimensional distribution is fundamental in nature, and has a wide range of applications. Efficient sampling algorithms underpin the utility of Monte Carlo approximation [ 39 , 42 ] ; support uncertainty quantification in Bayesian models [ 18 , 6 ] ; and lie at the heart of generative AI [ 40 , 16 , 54 , 13 ] . Recent years have witnessed tremendous practical and theoretical advances in the use of diffusion 1 1 1 In full generality, the diffusion terminology is a misnomer, since not all such models involve a diffusion process in the formal probabilistic sense; this includes the unmasking models studied in this paper. Nonetheless, we adopt the conventional terminology. sampling algorithms, which generate samples via a sequence of “denoising” operations [ 45 , 46 , 23 , 47 , 14 , 12 , 5 ] . Initial work in the area focused on sampling from continuous distributions in d , in which case the denoising step corresponds to estimating a signal embedded in Gaussian noise [ 23 , 47 ] . A more recent line of work, and the general focus of this paper, has focused on sampling from discrete distributions, using various kinds of denoising processes [ 24 , 3 , 9 , 31 , 44 , 43 , 15 , 17 ] . In this paper, we study the problem of sampling a random vector Z ∈ ( 𝒜 ) d Z\in(\mathcal{A})^{d} , where 𝒜 \mathcal{A} is a discrete alphabet, and d d is the ambient dimension. While various samplers have been devised, we focus on unmasking samplers , which traverse a path from a fully unobserved vector, denoted by Z ∗ = ( ⋆ , … , ⋆ ) Z^{*}=(\star,\ldots,\star) with ⋆ \star meaning masked or unobserved, back to a sample Z ∼ ℙ Z Z\sim\mathbb{P}_{Z} from the target distribution. The path is traversed via a sequence of unmasking operations, in which a subset of the masked coordinates are revealed. Unmasking algorithms differ in the form and sequence by which these unmasking steps take place. Unmasking and closely related mask-based generative samplers have proven effective across a range of applications, including machine translation [ 19 ] , image and video synthesis [ 11 , 55 ] , text-to-image generation [ 10 ] , speech synthesis [ 52 ] , language modeling [ 43 , 33 ] , and protein design [ 51 ] .

sections.heading: 1.1 Overview
sections.text: This paper is motivated by two broad questions associated with diffusion samplers, as articulated in our companion paper on Gaussian diffusion [ 50 ] , which we paraphrase here: Q1: Can the performance of masked diffusion sampling be explained and quantified, in some generality, by a measure tied to data geometry? Q2: Is it possible to exploit a masked-diffusion measure of data geometry to design, optimize and certify practical sampling schemes? Recent work has made substantial progress on both questions. Chen et al. [ 15 ] analyze fixed-cardinality unmasking and derive an exact information-profile representation of its expected KL discretization error, with consequences for schedule design and bounds based on total and dual total correlation. Lavenant and Zanella [ 25 ] derive an information-profile representation of the factorization error for random-order unmasking, and study optimal schedules in asymptotic scaling regimes. From a different direction, Dmitriev et al. [ 17 ] analyze discrete diffusion via a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) formulation; for masking diffusion, their modified τ \tau -leaping guarantees are governed by an effective total correlation that can be substantially smaller than the classical worst-case measures. Collectively, these results provide important answers to Q1 and partial answers to Q2 , but fall short of finite-sample guarantees for learning and certifying geometry-adaptive schedules from data. Our answer to Q1 is based on the unmasking growth complexity or UGC for short. It is a path-resolved measure of data dependence along the reveal process. We show that its local increments directly control KL discretization error, thereby obtaining a common analysis of both fixed-cardinality unmasking and a natural Bernoulli-subset variant. When collapsed over the full reveal path, the UGC complexity reduces to a coarse measure that closely connected to classical multivariate dependence measures [ 53 , 21 , 22 , 48 ] , as well as to the effective total correlation appearing in the CTMC analysis [ 17 ] . Consequently, the resulting single-block guarantees sharpen existing fixed-cardinality bounds while giving Bernoulli unmasking guarantees comparable to those available for CTMC samplers. The main contributions of our paper are in the context of Q2 , and in particular, our use of the full UGC complexity path to design and analyze sampling algorithms that are certified-optimal. More precisely, we show that UGC complexity has a natural additive structure along the reveal path, so that its local increments can be estimated from samples and used to allocate computational effort where the target distribution is most difficult to unmask. We exploit this structure to derive and optimize blockwise schedules, construct data-dependent samplers with high-probability KL certificates, and finally, to optimize the block boundaries themselves. In the fine-partition limit, the log-reveal-odds UGC density emerges as the intrinsic local geometry: its square-root integral governs the limiting partition complexity and the sharp leading-order optimal Euler discretization error.

sections.heading: 1.2 Related work
sections.text: So as to put our results in context, we now provide a broader discussion of related work. There are various types of discrete diffusion models, all of which replace the additive Gaussian noise for continuous-space diffusions by stochastic corruption kernels on discrete state spaces. Early work developed multinomial and more general structured discrete diffusion processes [ 24 , 3 ] , among them the absorbing-state corruption that underlies a masking diffusion process. Other work [ 9 ] formulated discrete diffusion models using the formalism of continuous-time Markov chains, with subsequent work developing discrete analogues of score-based modeling in which the reverse CTMC is parameterized through learned probability ratios [ 31 ] . Masked diffusion is a particularly important subclass, in which coordinates are corrupted by replacement with a distinguished mask symbol and generation proceeds by progressively reconstructing masked coordinates [ 44 , 43 ] . As described above, recent work has made progress on characterizing the accuracy–parallelism trade-off in random-order unmasking with fixed-cardinality subsets. In particular, Li and Cai [ 26 ] established information-theoretic convergence guarantees for parallel masked-diffusion sampling. Chen et al. [ 15 ] derived an exact characterization of the expected KL divergence in terms of a one-dimensional information profile; they also gave explicit sampling guarantees involving classical multivariate dependence measures [ 53 , 21 , 22 ] , namely the total correlation ( 𝖳𝖢 \mathsf{TC} ) and dual total correlation ( 𝖣𝖳𝖢 \mathsf{DTC} ). A portion of our analysis exploits their exact KL representation. Lavenant and Zanella [ 25 ] derived an information-profile representation for the factorization error of random-order unmasking, and then studied optimal scheduling via a continuum scaling limit. We compare their asymptotic schedule analysis more closely with our fine-partition and Euler results following Theorem 3 . The τ \tau -leaping method for continuous-time Markov chains (CTMC) originates in stochastic chemical kinetics, where its consistency and approximation errors have been studied extensively [ 20 , 36 , 27 , 2 ] . For discrete diffusion, recent work has developed convergence guarantees for τ \tau -leaping under both standard and absorbing corruption processes [ 37 , 28 , 29 , 17 ] , as well as higher-order variants of CTMC discretization [ 38 ] . Among CTMC analyses, most related to our work is the paper of Dmitriev et al. [ 17 ] , who analyze a modified τ \tau -leaping sampler for a general class of CTMC discrete diffusion models. For masking diffusion, they give guarantees in terms of a measure that they call effective total correlation, which turns out to be closely related to the coarse UGC complexity that we introduce. In contrast to CTMC-based analyses, we study Bernoulli and fixed-cardinality unmasking; our coarse UGC bounds yield matching guarantees for these direct schemes. The coarse UGC complexity is also connected to several multivariate dependence measures, including 𝖳𝖢 \mathsf{TC} , 𝖣𝖳𝖢 \mathsf{DTC} , and the finer-grained measure of Tononi et al. [ 48 ] . We develop these connections in Appendix A . Finally, in our companion paper [ 50 ] on Gaussian diffusion sampling, we introduced the denoising growth complexity ( DGC ), a pathwise complexity that controls KL discretization error, and whose log-scale DGC density specifies optimal sampling schedules. Despite the substantial differences between Gaussian and masking diffusion, the two theories exhibit a remarkable degree of parallelism, suggesting a common underlying principle linking denoising growth, KL discretization error, and optimal scheduling.

sections.heading: 2 Overview: unmasking growth complexity and sampling
sections.text: So as to orient the reader, we begin by providing a high-level overview of the main ideas and quantities underlying our analysis. We first describe the canonical unmasking process. Using it, we define the unmasking growth complexity ( UGC ), which measures how informational difficulty is distributed along the reveal path. We then pass to log-reveal-odds coordinates, where this complexity is represented by a density whose geometry determines how sampling effort should be allocated along the path. Our goal here is primarily conceptual: to explain the distinction between coarse and geometry-aware schedules, to illustrate the data geometry of the UGC density on several examples, and to preview how data-driven adaptive partitioning can exploit this geometry. Precise forms of our guarantees for samplers, estimation procedures, and supporting technical results are developed in the subsequent sections.

sections.heading: 2.2 Unmasking growth complexity and its geometry
sections.text: For a reveal time t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] , we define the Bernoulli unmasking gain 𝗁 ⁡ ( t ) \displaystyle\mathsf{h}(t) ≔ ∑ i = 1 d Info ⁡ ( Z i ; X t ∣ i ∈ ℳ ⁡ ( X t ) ) , \displaystyle\coloneqq\;\sum_{i=1}^{d}\operatorname{Info}\big(Z_{i};X_{t}\mid i\in\mathcal{M}(X_{t})\big), (2a) where ℳ ⁡ ( X t ) ⊆ { 1 , … , d } \mathcal{M}(X_{t})\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\} is the subset of indices that are masked at reveal time t t , and Info \operatorname{Info} denotes the (conditional) mutual information. The function 𝗁 \mathsf{h} has a denoising interpretation, since when i ∈ ℳ ⁡ ( X t ) i\in\mathcal{M}(X_{t}) , all other coordinates in X t X_{t} are revealed independently with probability t t ; the conditional mutual information term for the i t ​ h i^{th} coordinate measures how much these revealed variables reduce uncertainty about Z i Z_{i} . Moreover, the derivative 𝗁 ′ \mathsf{h}^{\prime} turns out to have a simple information-theoretic representation: in particular, it corresponds to the second derivative 𝗁 ′ ​ ( t ) \displaystyle\mathsf{h}^{\prime}(t) = − d 2 d ​ t 2 ​ Info ⁡ ( Z ; X t ) , \displaystyle=-\frac{d^{2}}{dt^{2}}\operatorname{Info}(Z;X_{t}), (2b) where Info ⁡ ( Z , X t ) \operatorname{Info}(Z;X_{t}) denotes the mutual information between the target vector Z ∈ 𝒜 d Z\in\mathcal{A}^{d} and the partially unmasked vector X t ∈ ( 𝒜 ∪ { ⋆ } ) d X_{t}\in\big(\mathcal{A}\cup\{\star\}\big)^{d} at reveal time t ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) t\in(0,1) . See equation ( 51a ) in the proof of Theorem 1 for the underlying details. In terms of this mutual information derivative, the unmasking growth complexity assigns a non-negative number to any sub-interval [ p , q ] [p,q] of the unit interval [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] via 𝖧 ⁡ ( p , q ) \displaystyle\mathsf{H}(p,q) ≔ ∫ p q t ( 1 − t ) 𝗁 ′ ( t ) d t for any 0 ≤ p < q ≤ 1 . \displaystyle\coloneqq\int_{p}^{q}t(1-t)\mathsf{h}^{\prime}(t)\,dt\quad\mbox{for any $0\leq p<q\leq 1$.} (2c) Based on the identity ( 2b ), we see that 𝖧 ⁡ ( p , q ) \mathsf{H}(p,q) is a weighted integral of the information curvature. The essential feature of this complexity measure is that it is a path-resolved quantity : rather than assigning a single complexity to the target distribution ℙ Z \mathbb{P}_{Z} , it assigns a complexity to every interval of the reveal path. Our analysis shows how these local increments directly control the associated KL discretization error. Moreover, for any triple 0 ≤ p < q < r ≤ 1 0\leq p<q<r\leq 1 , we have the additivity property 𝖧 ⁡ ( p , r ) \displaystyle\mathsf{H}(p,r) = 𝖧 ⁡ ( p , q ) + 𝖧 ⁡ ( q , r ) . \displaystyle=\mathsf{H}(p,q)+\mathsf{H}(q,r). (3) This additivity allows the global sampling problem to be decomposed into local pieces, whose complexities can be estimated and controlled separately, and is what ultimately enables geometry-adaptive refinement of the sampling schedule. By collapsing the path-resolved complexity to the full interval [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , we obtain the aggregate UGC mass given by 𝖧 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) = ∫ 0 1 t ⁡ ( 1 − t ) ​ 𝗁 ′ ​ ( t ) ​ 𝑑 t \mathsf{H}(0,1)=\int_{0}^{1}t(1-t)\mathsf{h}^{\prime}(t)dt . Interestingly, this aggregate quantity has several connections to classical measures of multivariate dependence. By a non-trivial argument (see the proof of Proposition 3 ), it turns out to be equivalent to a multivariate dependence measure, first introduced by Tononi, Sporns and Edelman [ 48 ] in 1994, which spawned a rich line of work (e.g., [ 7 , 8 , 34 , 4 , 41 , 49 ] ). A separate argument shows its close relation to the effective total correlation introduced by Dmitriev et al. [ 17 ] in their study of CTMC unmasking algorithms. Moreover, the value 𝖧 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \mathsf{H}(0,1) can be upper bounded by classical measures of multivariate dependence [ 53 , 21 , 22 ] , known as total correlation and dual total correlation. We elaborate upon these and other connections in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 2.2.1 Geometric behavior of UGC density
sections.text: Since the UGC density 𝗊 \mathsf{q} captures the essential structure of the problem, it is useful to compute and plot it for three different ensembles, each chosen to illustrate a qualitative aspect of our theory.

sections.heading: Noisy repeated bit:
sections.text: We begin with a very simple example. For any p ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] p\in[0,1] , we use V ∼ Ber ​ ( p ) V\sim\textsf{Ber}(p) to denote a Bernoulli random variable with ℙ ⁡ ( V = 1 ) = p \mathbb{P}(V=1)=p and ℙ ⁡ ( V = 0 ) = 1 − p \mathbb{P}(V=0)=1-p . sections.heading: Discrete mixture models:
sections.text: Our second ensemble corresponds to the discrete analog of a mixture model. This procedure generates an M M -component mixture distribution with uniform weight 1 / M 1/M on each component. (a) (b) (c) Figure 2: Plots of the log-reveal-odds UGC density 𝗊 \mathsf{q} for the discrete mixture model. For each dimension d d , the latent vector Z ∈ { 0 , 1 } d Z\in\{0,1\}^{d} is generated by selecting uniformly from M = 2 d / 4 M=2^{d/4} cluster centers, and then flipping each coordinate independently with probability η = 0.02 \eta=0.02 . Panels (a)–(c) correspond to d ∈ { 32 , 48 , 64 } d\in\{32,48,64\} , and hence M ∈ { 256 , 4096 , 65536 } M\in\{256,4096,65536\} , respectively. Increasing the dimension produces a progressively sharper and taller spike. Figure 2 shows a sequence of UGC densities for this family, with the dimension d d and the number M = 2 d / 4 M=2^{d/4} of mixture components increasing as we move from left to right. The density is unimodal in all cases; as the dimension increases, the peak location remains fixed but its height increases. It can be shown that the ratio ( 6 ) scales as Ratio ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) = Θ ~ ​ ( d ) \operatorname{Ratio}(\mathbb{P}_{Z})=\widetilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{d}) , so that there are significant gains from using geometry-aware stepsizes. Moreover, since the UGC density is concentrated around a single increasingly narrow transition window, a partition with only K = 3 K=3 blocks—one covering this transition and two covering its tails—achieves the fine-partition complexity up to logarithmic factors. See Section 2.2.2 and Figure 2 for further discussion of these factors.

sections.heading: Hierarchical mixture model:
sections.text: The previous examples, being quite simple in nature, all led to unimodal UGC densities. We now consider a hierarchical model in which multiple peaks emerge, and the peaks have interesting meanings in terms of the underlying data geometry. sections.heading: 2.2.2 From coarse to fine geometry
sections.text: Let us describe how we exploit finer-grained UGC geometry for algorithmic purposes. A single-block scheme uses one geometric multiplier across the full log-reveal-odds interval, and its performance is governed by the coarse complexity 𝖢 UGC \mathsf{C}_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{{UGC} }}} . In order to exploit local UGC geometry, we instead partition the interval [ − ℓ d , ℓ d ] [-\ell_{d},\ell_{d}] into K K blocks and allow a different geometric multiplier on each block. For a partition 𝒫 = { [ λ k , λ k + 1 ] } k = 0 K − 1 \mathcal{P}=\{[\lambda_{k},\lambda_{k+1}]\}_{k=0}^{K-1} , define the block lengths 𝖲 k = λ k + 1 − λ k \mathsf{S}_{k}=\lambda_{k+1}-\lambda_{k} and the associated UGC increments 𝖧 k = ∫ λ k λ k + 1 𝗊 ⁡ ( λ ) ​ 𝑑 λ \mathsf{H}_{k}=\int_{\lambda_{k}}^{\lambda_{k+1}}\mathsf{q}(\lambda)\,d\lambda . Optimizing the geometric multipliers over these blocks leads to the partition complexity 𝖢 ⁡ ( 𝒫 ) \displaystyle\mathsf{C}(\mathcal{P}) ≔ ( ∑ k = 0 K − 1 𝖲 k ​ 𝖧 k ) 2 . \displaystyle\coloneqq\left(\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\sqrt{\mathsf{S}_{k}\mathsf{H}_{k}}\right)^{2}. (7a) Proposition 1 shows that this quantity governs the iteration complexity of the resulting K K -block sampler. Although the optimal multipliers depend on the unknown increments 𝖧 k \mathsf{H}_{k} , these increments can be estimated from clean samples. We use these estimates to choose the partition and its multipliers from data, leading to the certified guarantees; see Proposition 2 and Theorem 2 . Progressive refinement interpolates between the coarse single-block complexity and the fine-partition limit ( 5b ). In particular, in Theorem 3 , we prove that inf 𝒫 𝖢 ⁡ ( 𝒫 ) = ( ∫ − ℓ d ℓ d 𝗊 ⁡ ( λ ) ​ 𝑑 λ ) 2 where the infimum is over partitions of [ − ℓ d , ℓ d ] . \displaystyle\inf_{\mathcal{P}}\mathsf{C}(\mathcal{P})\;=\;\Big(\int_{-\ell_{d}}^{\ell_{d}}\sqrt{\mathsf{q}(\lambda)}d\lambda\Big)^{2}\qquad\mbox{where the infimum is over partitions of $[-\ell_{d},\ell_{d}]$.} (7b) Thus, increasing the number of blocks allows the sampler to exploit increasingly fine features of the local UGC geometry, and ultimately achieve the fine-grained complexity based on 𝗊 \sqrt{\mathsf{q}} .

sections.heading: 3 Unmasking samplers and KL discretization error
sections.text: We now turn to the description and analysis of some simple unmasking samplers. At a high level, they are based on discretized approximations to the unmasking reveal process { X t , t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] } \{X_{t},t\in[0,1]\} from equation ( 1b ). Recalling that ℳ ⁡ ( x ) \mathcal{M}(x) denotes the set of masked coordinates in the vector x x , their updates involve the single-site posterior distributions μ i ​ ( a , x ) \displaystyle\mu_{i}(a,x) ≔ ℙ ( Z i = a ∣ Z j = x j for all j ∉ ℳ ⁡ ( x ) ) , defined for each i ∈ ℳ ⁡ ( x ) , \displaystyle\coloneqq\mathbb{P}\big(Z_{i}=a\mid Z_{j}=x_{j}\quad\mbox{for all $j\notin\mathcal{M}(x)$}\big),\quad\mbox{defined for each $i\in\mathcal{M}(x)$,} (8) where a ∈ 𝒜 a\in\mathcal{A} and x ∈ ( 𝒜 ∪ { ⋆ } ) d x\in\big(\mathcal{A}\cup\{\star\}\big)^{d} . We use μ \mu to denote the full collection of these distributions, and often refer to it as the denoiser . It summarizes residual uncertainty in Z Z given the observation x x . In practice, the denoiser μ \mu is estimated based on samples from ℙ Z \mathbb{P}_{Z} as follows. Given a clean sample Z ∼ ℙ Z Z\sim\mathbb{P}_{Z} , we can generate training examples by independently masking random subsets of coordinates. We then predict the original value of each masked coordinate from the resulting partially observed sample using cross-entropy loss. With this set-up, the population-optimal predictors are given by the posterior distributions μ i ​ ( ⋅ , x ) \mu_{i}(\mathord{\cdot},x) , and the training procedure generates estimates μ ^ i \widehat{\mu}_{i} for each i = 1 , … , d i=1,\ldots,d . For simplicity, we describe the algorithms using the exact denoiser μ \mu . Using a learned denoiser μ ^ \widehat{\mu} contributes an additional term to the KL error bound in a standard way; see equation ( 18 ) following the statement of Theorem 1 for details.

sections.heading: 3.1 Bernoulli and fixed-cardinality unmasking
sections.text: We now describe the two standard unmasking samplers that we analyze in this paper. At a high level, they involve two basic operations: choosing a subset of indices and then, conditional on this subset, making a random choice of values for the revealed variables using the denoiser μ \mu . The samplers that we analyze differ only in how the random subset is chosen: the Bernoulli sampler uses coin flips, thereby generating a set with a random cardinality, whereas the fixed-cardinality sampler chooses a random subset with fixed cardinality. Both samplers are used in practice, and our theory gives a unified analysis of both in terms of UGC functions. Given a subset A ⊆ [ d ] A\subseteq[d] of coordinates, both samplers make use of the conditional distribution ℙ umask ​ ( X ′ ∣ X , A ) \displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{umask}}}(X^{\prime}\mid X,A) ≔ ( ⨂ i ∉ ℳ ⁡ ( X ) δ X i ) ⊗ ( ⨂ i ∈ A μ i ​ ( ⋅ , X ) ) ⊗ ( ⨂ i ∈ ℳ ⁡ ( X ) ∖ A δ ⋆ ) , for A ⊆ ℳ ⁡ ( X ) , \displaystyle\coloneqq\Big(\bigotimes_{i\notin\mathcal{M}(X)}\delta_{X_{i}}\Big)\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{i\in A}\mu_{i}(\mathord{\cdot},X)\right)\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{i\in\mathcal{M}(X)\setminus A}\delta_{\star}\right),\qquad\mbox{for $A\subseteq\mathcal{M}(X)$,} (9a) which fixes all observed variables (i.e., indices i ∉ ℳ ⁡ ( X ) i\notin\mathcal{M}(X) ); fixes all missing variables not in A A ; and makes a random update to variables in A A . Moreover, for an iteration count N ≥ 1 N\geq 1 , both samplers are based on a reveal-time grid 0 < t 0 < t 1 < ⋯ < t N < 1 . \displaystyle 0<t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{N}<1. (9b) The samplers are initialized with a random choice X ^ 0 ∼ ℚ t 0 \widehat{X}^{0}\sim\mathbb{Q}_{t_{0}} , and then generate a sequence { X ^ j } j = 0 N \{\widehat{X}^{j}\}_{j=0}^{N} moving forward in time across the grid ( 9b ).

sections.heading: 3.1.1 Bernoulli unmasking sampler
sections.text: We begin by describing the Bernoulli unmasking sampler. It chooses subsets according to the binomial distribution ℙ Ber ​ ( A ∣ X , β ) \displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{Ber}}}(A\mid X,\beta) ≔ β card ⁡ ( A ) ( 1 − β ) card ⁡ ( ℳ ⁡ ( X ) ∖ A ) with support A ⊆ ℳ ⁡ ( X ) , \displaystyle\coloneqq\beta^{\operatorname{card}(A)}(1-\beta)^{\operatorname{card}(\mathcal{M}(X)\setminus A)}\qquad\mbox{with support $A\subseteq\mathcal{M}(X)$,} (10) and then updates entries according to the conditional distribution ( 9a ). More precisely, given the initialization X ^ 0 \widehat{X}^{0} and reveal-time grid ( 9b ), it generates the sequence Draw random binomial subset: A j ∼ ℙ Ber ​ ( ⋅ ∣ X ^ j , β j ) , where ​ β j ≔ t j + 1 − t j 1 − t j , \displaystyle\quad A^{j}\sim\mathbb{P}_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{Ber}}}\big(\mathord{\cdot}\mid\widehat{X}^{j},\beta_{j}\big),\qquad\mbox{where }\beta_{j}\coloneqq\frac{t_{j+1}-t_{j}}{1-t_{j}}, (11a) Random unmasking: X ^ j + 1 ∼ ℙ umask ​ ( ⋅ ∣ X ^ j , A j ) , \displaystyle\quad\widehat{X}^{j+1}\sim\mathbb{P}_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{umask}}}\big(\mathord{\cdot}\mid\widehat{X}^{j},A^{j}\big), (11b) for iterations j = 0 , 1 , … , N − 1 j=0,1,\ldots,N-1 .

sections.heading: 3.1.2 Fixed-cardinality unmasking sampler
sections.text: The fixed-cardinality sampler is very similar, except that it replaces the binomial subset choice ( 10 ) with a black-box that draws a uniformly random subset of a specified size. More precisely, the fixed-cardinality sampler only admits iteration counts N < d − 1 N<d-1 , and it requires that each reveal time be d d -aligned, meaning that t j = s j / d t_{j}=s_{j}/d for integers 1 ≤ s 0 < ⋯ < s N ≤ d − 1 1\leq s_{0}<\cdots<s_{N}\leq d-1 . It initializes X ^ 0 \widehat{X}^{0} with exactly d − s 0 d-s_{0} masked coordinates. Then, at iteration j = 0 , … , N − 1 j=0,\ldots,N-1 , the current state X ^ j \widehat{X}^{j} has exactly d − s j d-s_{j} masked coordinates. Draw fixed-cardinality subset: A j ∼ Unif ⁡ { A ⊆ ℳ ⁡ ( X ^ j ) | card ⁡ ( A ) = s j + 1 − s j } . \displaystyle\qquad A^{j}\sim\operatorname{Unif}\Big\{A\subseteq\mathcal{M}(\widehat{X}^{j})\,\Big|\,\operatorname{card}(A)=s_{j+1}-s_{j}\Big\}. (12a) Random unmasking: X ^ j + 1 ∼ ℙ umask ​ ( ⋅ ∣ X ^ j , A j ) , \displaystyle\quad\widehat{X}^{j+1}\sim\mathbb{P}_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{umask}}}\big(\mathord{\cdot}\mid\widehat{X}^{j},A^{j}\big), (12b) For future reference, we note that underlying the fixed-cardinality sampler is a de-Poissonized version of the unmasking process { X t , t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] } \{X_{t},t\in[0,1]\} . It is defined only at d d -aligned times t = s / d t=s/d , and the associated variable X t ∼ ℙ t has exactly s revealed coordinates, \displaystyle X_{t}\sim\mathbb{P}_{t}\qquad\mbox{has exactly $s$ revealed coordinates,} (13) for a subset of cardinality s s chosen uniformly at random. Note that we are overloading our notation here, but the specific version of ℙ t \mathbb{P}_{t} being used will be clear from context.

sections.text: Both samplers involve initialization and completion steps. In our analysis, the initialization cost is measured by the KL divergence D KL ( ℙ t 0 ∥ ℚ t 0 ) where X t 0 ∼ ℙ t 0 and X ^ 0 ∼ ℚ t 0 . \displaystyle D_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{KL}}}(\mathbb{P}_{{t_{0}}}\|\mathbb{Q}_{{t_{0}}})\qquad\mbox{where $X_{t_{0}}\sim\mathbb{P}_{t_{0}}$ and $\widehat{X}^{0}\sim\mathbb{Q}_{{t_{0}}}$.} (14a) Here X t 0 X_{t_{0}} is generated by the standard reveal process for the Bernoulli sampler ( 1b ), and from its de-Poissonized analogue ( 13 ) for the fixed-cardinality sampler. Moreover, both samplers involve a final completion step, based on a completion kernel 𝖢 T ​ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) \mathsf{C}_{T}(\mathord{\cdot}\mid x) that maps each partially revealed terminal state x ∈ ( 𝒜 ∪ { ⋆ } ) d x\in\big(\mathcal{A}\cup\{\star\}\big)^{d} to a probability law on fully specified vectors in 𝒜 d \mathcal{A}^{d} . The defect of any completion kernel is measured by Γ 𝖢 ​ ( T ) \displaystyle\Gamma_{\mathsf{C}}(T) ≔ 𝔼 X T ​ [ D KL ​ ( ℒ ⁡ ( Z ∣ X T ) ∥ 𝖢 T ​ ( ⋅ ∣ X T ) ) ] . \displaystyle\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{X_{T}}\left[D_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{KL}}}\left(\mathcal{L}(Z\mid X_{T})\,\middle\|\,\mathsf{C}_{T}(\mathord{\cdot}\mid X_{T})\right)\right]. (14b) While these terms appear in our bounds, they are not dominant terms. With the endpoint T = d − 1 d T=\frac{d-1}{d} , we have card ⁡ ( ℳ ⁡ ( X T ) ) = 1 \operatorname{card}(\mathcal{M}(X_{T}))=1 for the exact cardinality sampler and 𝔼 ⁡ [ card ⁡ ( ℳ ⁡ ( X T ) ) ] = 1 \mathbb{E}[\operatorname{card}(\mathcal{M}(X_{T}))]=1 for the Bernoulli sampler, so that the computational cost of implementing this completion kernel is minimal. sections.heading: 3.2 Unified analysis
sections.text: We are now set up to state a single theorem that provides a unified analysis of both the Bernoulli and fixed-cardinality unmasking samplers. Our original definition ( 2a ) of the Bernoulli denoising gain 𝗁 \mathsf{h} emphasizes the connection to the reveal process. Here, in order to make transparent the connections with fixed-cardinality sampling, we make use of the following equivalent representation: 𝗁 ⁡ ( t ) \displaystyle\mathsf{h}(t) = ∑ i = 1 d 𝔼 A i , t ​ [ Info ⁡ ( Z i ; Z A i , t ) ] , \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathbb{E}_{A_{i,t}}\big[\operatorname{Info}(Z_{i};Z_{A_{i,t}})\big], (15a) where A i , t ⊆ [ d ] ∖ { i } A_{i,t}\subseteq[d]\setminus\{i\} is a random subset obtained by including each coordinate of [ d ] ∖ { i } [d]\setminus\{i\} independently with probability t t . See Appendix B for the proof of this alternative representation. The analogue for the fixed-cardinality sampler is given by the fixed-cardinality unmasking gain coefficients 𝗁 j card \displaystyle\mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j} ≔ ∑ i = 1 d 𝔼 B i , j [ Info ( Z i ; Z B i , j ) ] where B i , j is uniform over j -cardinality subsets of [ d ] ∖ { i } . \displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathbb{E}_{B_{i,j}}\big[\operatorname{Info}(Z_{i};Z_{B_{i,j}})\big]\qquad\mbox{where $B_{i,j}$ is uniform over $j$-cardinality subsets of $[d]\setminus\{i\}$.} (15b) These coefficients are defined for j = 1 , … , d − 1 j=1,\ldots,d-1 , with 𝗁 0 card ≔ 0 \mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{0}\coloneqq 0 . These two notions lead to the two versions of UGC growth complexity , given by Bernoulli: 𝖧 ( p , q ) \displaystyle\mbox{{\lx@text@underline{Bernoulli:}}}\qquad\mathsf{H}(p,q) ≔ ∫ p q t ( 1 − t ) 𝗁 ′ ( t ) d t for pairs 0 ≤ p < q ≤ 1 , and \displaystyle\coloneqq\int_{p}^{q}t(1-t)\mathsf{h}^{\prime}(t)\,dt\qquad\mbox{for pairs $0\leq p<q\leq 1$, and} (16a) Exact cardinality: 𝖧 card ( a , b ) \displaystyle\mbox{{\lx@text@underline{Exact cardinality:}}}\qquad\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{card}}(a,b) ≔ ∑ j = a + 1 b − 1 ( j d ) ​ ( 1 − j d ) ​ { 𝗁 j card − 𝗁 j − 1 card } , 0 ≤ a < b ≤ d . \displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{j=a+1}^{b-1}\left(\frac{j}{d}\right)\left(1-\frac{j}{d}\right)\big\{\mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j}-\mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j-1}\big\},\qquad 0\leq a<b\leq d. (16b) Our main theorem bounds the KL error of both the Bernoulli and fixed-cardinality unmasking samplers in terms of increments of these respective UGC functions. It applies to any reveal-time grid ( 9b ), and the analysis shows why the reveal odds function ψ ⁡ ( t ) ≔ t 1 − t \psi(t)\coloneqq\frac{t}{1-t} is natural. Theorem 1 . For any grid ( 9b ), the Ber -unmasking sampler produces output Z ^ \widehat{Z} such that D KL ​ ( ℙ Z ∥ ℙ Z ^ ) \displaystyle D_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{KL}}}\left(\mathbb{P}_{Z}\,\middle\|\,\mathbb{P}_{\widehat{Z}}\right) ≤ ∑ j = 0 N − 1 { ψ ⁡ ( t j + 1 ) ψ ⁡ ( t j ) − 1 } 𝖧 ( t j , t j + 1 ) + D KL ( ℙ t 0 ∥ ℚ t 0 ) + Γ 𝖢 ( T ) . \displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\left\{\frac{\psi(t_{j+1})}{\psi(t_{j})}-1\right\}\mathsf{H}(t_{j},t_{j+1})+D_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{KL}}}(\mathbb{P}_{t_{0}}\|\mathbb{Q}_{t_{0}})+\Gamma_{\mathsf{C}}(T). (17a) Moreover, for any d d -aligned grid t j = a j d t_{j}=\frac{a_{j}}{d} , the Card -unmasking sampler produces output Z ^ card \widehat{Z}^{\mathrm{card}} such that D KL ​ ( ℙ Z ∥ ℙ Z ^ card ) \displaystyle D_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{KL}}}\left(\mathbb{P}_{Z}\,\middle\|\,\mathbb{P}_{\widehat{Z}^{\mathrm{card}}}\right) ≤ ∑ j = 0 N − 1 { ψ ⁡ ( t j + 1 ) ψ ⁡ ( t j + 1 d ) − 1 } 𝖧 card ( a j , a j + 1 ) + D KL ( ℙ t 0 ∥ ℚ t 0 ) + Γ 𝖢 ( T ) . \displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\left\{\frac{\psi(t_{j+1})}{\psi\big(t_{j}+\tfrac{1}{d}\big)}-1\right\}\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{card}}(a_{j},a_{j+1})+D_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{KL}}}(\mathbb{P}_{t_{0}}\|\mathbb{Q}_{t_{0}})+\Gamma_{\mathsf{C}}(T). (17b) We prove these two claims in Sections 6.1 and 6.2 , respectively. The proofs are relatively short, and follow the same template of starting from an exact representation of the KL discretization error over the interval, and then bounding it in terms of 𝖧 \mathsf{H} or 𝖧 card \mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{card}} respectively. For the Bernoulli sampler, we first derive the exact KL representation, from which the upper bound ( 17a ) follows from an elementary argument. On the other hand, the fixed-cardinality guarantee ( 17b ) makes use of the exact representation of the KL discretization error, derived by Chen et al. [ 15 ] ; in particular, the coefficients 𝗁 j card \mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j} are rescaled versions of their information coefficients. In contrast to our upper bounds, neither form of the exact KL error has simple additive structure in terms of the log-reveal odds. This structure in our upper bounds turns out to be very useful: as we discuss in the sequel (see Corollary 1 and Appendix A ), a simple stepsize choice in the bound ( 17b ) gives an immediate sharpening of the fixed-cardinality sampling guarantees given in the paper [ 15 ] . sections.heading: 3.3.2 Some consequences
sections.text: At a high level, Corollary 1 and its analogue for fixed-cardinality sampling show that the iteration complexity when using a single geometric multiplier protocol is governed by the aggregate UGC mass functionals 𝖧 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \mathsf{H}(0,1) and 𝖧 card ​ ( 0 , d ) \mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{card}}(0,d) , respectively, for the Bernoulli and fixed-cardinality versions. These relations allow us to recover and sharpen several existing results on unmasking samplers. As we show in Appendix A , the aggregate UGC complexities associated with Bernoulli and fixed-cardinality unmasking are equivalent up to universal constants, and they are closely related to the complexity governing the CTMC guarantees of Dmitriev et al. [ 17 ] . Consequently, the single-block guarantee in Corollary 1 yields comparable guarantees for these different unmasking mechanisms, while sharpening bounds based only on total correlation and dual total correlation. We defer these comparisons, together with further information-theoretic aspects of aggregate UGC , to Appendix A .

sections.heading: 4 Certified-optimal bounds for the UGC path
sections.text: Thus far, we have considered the single-block consequence of Theorem 1 , based on one geometric multiplier over the full reveal interval. The additivity ( 3 ) of the UGC function allows a more refined approach. We first partition the reveal interval into K K blocks, and then optimize the stepsizes within each block. Doing so leads to a UGC partition complexity that refines the coarse UGC bound. We then show how the required UGC increments can be estimated from samples, yielding certified data-dependent samplers and allowing the block boundaries themselves to be optimized. Finally, by refining the partition, we recover the fine-partition complexity 𝖯 UGC \mathsf{P}_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathrm{{UGC} }}} in equation ( 5b ), which characterizes the optimal discretization error up to a factor of two.

sections.heading: Interpretation of the tail condition:
sections.text: Condition ( 33a ) controls the tails of the aggregate change in the one-coordinate denoisers over each reveal-odds-dyadic interval. This choice is important: it measures the same posterior changes that enter the trajectory statistic ( 32b ), rather than the absolute uncertainty of the individual denoisers. A condition on the true-symbol log loss, for instance, could be large even when revealing additional coordinates produces no change in any posterior. As a basic example, suppose that the coordinates of Z Z are independent. For the exact Bayes denoisers considered here, the forced-mask observation X t | i X_{t\mid i} reveals only masking variables and a subset of the coordinates Z − i Z_{-i} . sections.heading: 4.4 Sampling schemes that are certified-optimal
sections.text: In this section, we turn to the key problem of designing samplers that are certified-optimal , meaning that their iteration complexity meets the optimum specified by the partition complexity functional, up to data-dependent residual terms, and that for any target accuracy ε > 0 \varepsilon>0 and failure probability η ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \eta\in(0,1) , there are data-dependent parameter choices for the sampler guaranteeing that its output Z ^ \widehat{Z} satisfies the accuracy bound D KL ( ℙ Z ∥ ℙ Z ^ ) \displaystyle D_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{KL}}}\big(\mathbb{P}_{Z}\|\mathbb{P}_{\hat{Z}}\big) ≤ ε with probability at least 1 − η . \displaystyle\leq\varepsilon\qquad\mbox{with probability at least $1-\eta$.} (35) In Section 4.4.1 , we specify and analyze a certified procedure for a given K K -block partition, whereas in Section 4.4.2 , we describe certified procedures based on dynamic programming for choosing the block boundaries.

sections.heading: 5 Fine partition limit and optimal Euler discretization
sections.text: In the preceding section, we developed and analyzed sampling methods based on finite K K -block partitions, and showed how their performance depends on the local UGC mass of the chosen partition. We now characterize the limit under arbitrarily fine refinement and connect it to the optimal KL error of Euler discretization. This analysis highlights the central role of the log-reveal-odds UGC density 𝗊 \mathsf{q} defined in equation ( 4 ).

sections.heading: Related work:
sections.text: A related square-root principle appears in the analysis of Lavenant and Zanella [ 25 ] , who study random-order fixed-cardinality unmasking and express its factorization error in terms of a cardinality-indexed information profile. They then consider a high-dimensional continuum limit in which, using our notation, both the ambient dimension d d and the number of sampling rounds N N diverge. In the regime d / N → + ∞ d/N\rightarrow+\infty , optimization of the resulting limiting functional yields a square-root information-profile rule. Our results differ in both formulation and scope. The UGC density 𝗊 \mathsf{q} is defined directly from the finite-dimensional reveal path, with log-reveal odds providing the natural path coordinate, and our finite-step bounds apply at fixed dimension and for arbitrary finite partitions. Moreover, rather than optimizing only a limiting variational problem, we optimize blockwise schedules at finite dimension, and use estimated UGC increments to construct data-dependent partitions with certified guarantees. Finally, equation ( 41b ) gives the sharp leading-order optimal Euler error at fixed dimension d d as the number of discretization steps N N grows.

sections.text: We first ask how much can be gained by exploiting the local UGC geometry, and then how many blocks are needed to realize this gain. (42) For the repeated-bit and parity models (see Figure 5 ), we have Ratio ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) ≍ log ⁡ ( d ) \operatorname{Ratio}(\mathbb{P}_{Z})\asymp\log(d) , yielding a growing but relatively modest separation. For example, the discrete mixture model in Figure 2 satisfies Ratio ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) = Ω ~ ​ ( d ) \operatorname{Ratio}(\mathbb{P}_{Z})=\widetilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{d}) with high probability over the cluster centers. sections.heading: 5.2.2 Uniform partitions: a generic convergence bound
sections.text: The XORSAT example shows that a small number of well-placed blocks can already be near-optimal. For comparison, let 𝒰 K \mathcal{U}_{K} denote the uniform K K -block partition of [ − ℓ d , ℓ d ] [-\ell_{d},\ell_{d}] , which ignores local geometry when choosing the block boundaries. Here we quantify its convergence to the fine-partition limit under a simple global regularity condition. In particular, suppose that 𝖿 ≔ 𝗊 \mathsf{f}\coloneqq\sqrt{\mathsf{q}} is continuous on [ − ℓ d , ℓ d ] [-\ell_{d},\ell_{d}] , and define its modulus of continuity by ω 𝖿 ​ ( h ) \displaystyle\omega_{\mathsf{f}}(h) ≔ sup λ , λ ′ | 𝖿 ( λ ) − 𝖿 ( λ ′ ) | where the sup ranges over pairs λ , λ ′ ∈ [ − ℓ d , ℓ d ] with | λ − λ ′ | ≤ h . \displaystyle\coloneqq\sup_{\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}}|\mathsf{f}(\lambda)-\mathsf{f}(\lambda^{\prime})|\qquad\mbox{where the sup ranges over pairs $\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}\in[-\ell_{d},\ell_{d}]$ with $|\lambda-\lambda^{\prime}|\leq h$.} (45) Lemma 3 (Accuracy of uniform K K -block approximations) . For the uniform partition 𝒰 K \mathcal{U}_{K} , we have 𝖢 UGC ​ ( 𝒰 K ) \displaystyle\sqrt{\mathsf{C}_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{{UGC} }}}(\mathcal{U}_{K})} ≤ 𝖯 UGC ​ ( ℐ full ) + ℓ d ​ ω 𝖿 ​ ( 2 ​ ℓ d K ) . \displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\mathsf{P}_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathrm{{UGC} }}}(\mathcal{I}_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{full}}})}+\ell_{d}\,\omega_{\mathsf{f}}\left(\frac{2\ell_{d}}{K}\right). (46) The proof is the same modulus-of-continuity argument used for Gaussian diffusion in our companion paper (Lemma 4, [ 50 ] ). As a particular consequence, if 𝖿 \mathsf{f} is Lipschitz with constant Lip ⁡ ( 𝖿 ) \operatorname{Lip}(\mathsf{f}) , then 𝖢 UGC ​ ( 𝒰 K ) \displaystyle\sqrt{\mathsf{C}_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{{UGC} }}}(\mathcal{U}_{K})} ≤ 𝖯 UGC ​ ( ℐ full ) + 2 ​ Lip ⁡ ( 𝖿 ) ​ ℓ d 2 K . \displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\mathsf{P}_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathrm{{UGC} }}}(\mathcal{I}_{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{full}}})}+\frac{2\operatorname{Lip}(\mathsf{f})\ell_{d}^{2}}{K}. (47) This generic bound can be conservative because it depends on a global regularity constant and fixes the block boundaries in advance. For the XORSAT example, the Lipschitz constant Lip ⁡ ( 𝖿 ) \operatorname{Lip}(\mathsf{f}) grows with dimension even though K = 3 K=3 adaptively placed blocks are near-optimal. When samples are available, the data-dependent DP procedure in Section 4.4.2 instead optimizes the block boundaries directly.

sections.heading: 6 Proofs
sections.text: In this section, we collect the proofs of a subset of our results, including the proof of Theorem 1 , with the Bernoulli and fixed-cardinality versions given in Section 6.1 and Section 6.2 , respectively; the proof of our data-certification procedures, including Lemma 1 and Proposition 2 in Section 6.3 ; the proof of Theorem 2 in Section 6.4 ; and finally, the proof of Theorem 3 in Section 6.5 . We defer the proofs of other results in the paper to the appendices.

sections.heading: 7 Discussion
sections.text: In this paper, we have shown that the unmasking growth complexity ( UGC ) controls the performance of random subset unmasking schemes, and reveals the structure required to optimize their performance. It is a path-based measure with additive local increments that bound the corresponding KL discretization errors. The reveal odds determine the natural multiplicative scale for a finite unmasking step, making log-reveal-odds the appropriate path coordinate. The log-reveal-odds UGC density gives a local description of sampling difficulty: regions carrying little UGC mass can be traversed rapidly with large stepsizes, whereas regions of concentrated mass require smaller stepsizes. We formalized this resource-allocation principle via a notion of partition complexity . At one extreme, it reduces to a (coarse) single-block complexity; under progressive refinement, it converges to a functional of the square root of the UGC density, which also determines the sharp leading-order complexity of optimally scheduled Euler discretization. Notably, this paper moves beyond treating the underlying geometry as an oracle quantity. We show how the UGC increments can be reliably estimated using KL increments along a coupled reveal trajectory. By doing so, we obtain sampling methods that are certified-optimal , meaning that they are certified (with high probability) to achieve a pre-specified KL error, and their iteration complexity is within a constant factor of the optimal iteration complexity. Thus, our analysis connects three core tasks in diffusion sampling: characterizing the geometry of the target distribution, designing a sampling schedule, and certifying the accuracy of the resulting sampler. Let us make note of some important qualifications to this conclusion. Our strongest data-dependent guarantees rely on access to Bayes denoisers and on moment control for their KL increments. With learned denoisers, approximation error contributes an additional term to the KL guarantee, and it needs to be estimated for a fully certified guarantee. Moreover, our notion of optimality is relative to frozen-poster Euler discretizations. It is possible that higher-order discretizations and other more sophisticated procedures could admit different local geometries, and hence potentially different optimal clocks for stepsize allocation. This paper has focused exclusively on the utility of UGC complexity for designing and optimizing unmasking samplers. However, thinking beyond the context of sampling, the view of data geometry afforded by the UGC density is of independent interest for statistical analysis. As a notable example, Figure 3 shows the UGC density 𝗊 \mathsf{q} for a discrete mixture model with a hierarchical structure, where the 𝗊 \mathsf{q} -modes correspond to reveal times at which successive levels of the hierarchy are resolved. Our methods allow us to reliably estimate increments of the UGC density, and it would be interesting to do so for real-world discrete datasets. In our companion paper [ 50 ] on Gaussian diffusion sampling, we introduced the denoising growth complexity ( DGC ), and provided analogous results on sampling performance and stepsize optimization, again culminating in a characterization via the DGC density. Despite the substantial differences between Gaussian diffusion and discrete masking, the two theories exhibit a striking parallel. The natural path coordinates differ (log-heat-time versus log-reveal-odds), but both the UGC and DGC densities capture a form of information curvature along the noising path, and their shape dictates how computational effort should be allocated.

sections.heading: Appendix A Consequences of single-block theory
sections.text: In this appendix, we discuss some consequences of Corollary 1 , which gives single-block stepsize schedules with iteration complexity depending on the aggregate UGC masses 𝖧 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \mathsf{H}(0,1) and 𝖧 card ​ ( 0 , d ) \mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{card}}(0,d) , for the Bernoulli and fixed-cardinality samplers, respectively. For this reason, it is interesting to relate the aggregate UGC mass to other complexity measures, and thereby to relate these complexity measures to the sampling guarantees in the papers [ 15 , 17 ] . We begin by observing that the aggregate UGC mass 𝖧 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \mathsf{H}(0,1) turns out to be equivalent to a measure of multivariate dependence first introduced by Tononi, Sporns, and Edelman [ 48 ] for modeling brain function. This complexity measure, hereafter referred to as 𝖳𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{TSE} , has since been studied by various authors [ 34 , 4 , 41 , 49 ] , and also extended to a more general notion of intricacy [ 7 , 8 ] . The 𝖳𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{TSE} complexity is given by 𝖳𝖲𝖤 ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) \displaystyle\mathsf{TSE}(\mathbb{P}_{Z}) ≔ ∑ k = 1 d ( e k − k d e d ) where e k ≔ 𝔼 ⁡ [ Ent ⁡ ( Z A k ) ] , \displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{k=1}^{d}\left(e_{k}-\frac{k}{d}e_{d}\right)\qquad\mbox{where $e_{k}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\big[\operatorname{Ent}(Z_{A_{k}})\big]$,} (60) with A k A_{k} being a uniformly random subset of [ d ] [d] with k k elements. We establish its equivalence to the aggregate UGC mass as part of Proposition 3 below. Turning to sampling connections, the paper [ 15 ] analyzed the fixed-cardinality sampler, and gave guarantees in terms of the minimum of two classical measures of multivariate dependence [ 53 , 21 , 22 ] , known as the total correlation and dual total correlation , defined by 𝖳𝖢 ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) ≔ ∑ i = 1 d Ent ⁡ ( Z i ) − Ent ⁡ ( Z ) and 𝖣𝖳𝖢 ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) ≔ Ent ⁡ ( Z ) − ∑ i = 1 d Ent ⁡ ( Z i ∣ Z − i ) . \displaystyle\mathsf{TC}(\mathbb{P}_{Z})\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{d}\operatorname{Ent}(Z_{i})-\operatorname{Ent}(Z)\quad\mbox{and}\quad\mathsf{DTC}(\mathbb{P}_{Z})\coloneqq\operatorname{Ent}(Z)-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\operatorname{Ent}(Z_{i}\mid Z_{-i}). (61a) Here Ent \operatorname{Ent} denotes the Shannon entropy, whereas Z − i Z_{-i} denotes the ( d − 1 ) (d-1) -dimensional subvector of all coordinates except the i t ​ h i^{th} . The single-block sampling guarantee in terms of 𝖧 card ​ ( 0 , d ) \mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{card}}(0,d) , or equivalently 𝖧 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \mathsf{H}(0,1) , sharpens these guarantees for the fixed-cardinality sampler. As we show in Section B.2 , in particular via a Bernstein polynomial representation, the total and dual total correlation measures have the simple representations 𝖳𝖢 ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) = ∫ 0 1 ( 1 − t ) ​ 𝗁 ′ ​ ( t ) ​ 𝑑 t and 𝖣𝖳𝖢 ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) = ∫ 0 1 t ​ 𝗁 ′ ​ ( t ) ​ 𝑑 t . \displaystyle\mathsf{TC}(\mathbb{P}_{Z})=\int_{0}^{1}(1-t)\mathsf{h}^{\prime}(t)dt\quad\mbox{and}\quad\mathsf{DTC}(\mathbb{P}_{Z})=\int_{0}^{1}t\mathsf{h}^{\prime}(t)dt. (61b) Since 𝖧 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) = ∫ 0 1 t ⁡ ( 1 − t ) ​ 𝗁 ′ ​ ( t ) ​ 𝑑 t \mathsf{H}(0,1)=\int_{0}^{1}t\,(1-t)\mathsf{h}^{\prime}(t)dt , we see immediately that 𝖧 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \displaystyle\mathsf{H}(0,1) ≤ min ⁡ { 𝖳𝖢 ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) , 𝖣𝖳𝖢 ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) } . \displaystyle\leq\min\{\mathsf{TC}(\mathbb{P}_{Z}),\mathsf{DTC}(\mathbb{P}_{Z})\}. (61c) In their work on continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) sampling, Dmitriev et al. [ 17 ] gave a CTMC unmasking sampler with iteration complexity controlled by a functional 𝖣𝖧𝖶 ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) \mathsf{DHW}(\mathbb{P}_{Z}) , which they refer to as effective total correlation, that is also upper bounded by the minimum of the 𝖳𝖢 \mathsf{TC} and 𝖣𝖳𝖢 \mathsf{DTC} complexities. We also show as part of Proposition 3 that this functional is lower bounded by 𝖧 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \mathsf{H}(0,1) , and can be upper bounded by a constant multiple of it. Thus, both the Bernoulli and fixed-cardinality samplers, in their single-block instantiation, inherit the guarantees of the DHW analysis. In particular, their paper studies various interesting examples, including stochastic block models and quantized versions of low-dimensional structure, for which 𝖣𝖧𝖶 ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) \mathsf{DHW}(\mathbb{P}_{Z}) , and hence 𝖧 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \mathsf{H}(0,1) and 𝖧 card ​ ( 0 , d ) \mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{card}}(0,d) , are relatively small. Notably, they construct an instance with min ⁡ { 𝖳𝖢 ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) , 𝖣𝖳𝖢 ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) } = Θ ⁡ ( d ) \min\{\mathsf{TC}(\mathbb{P}_{Z}),\mathsf{DTC}(\mathbb{P}_{Z})\}=\Theta(d) , whereas their complexity has constant scaling. Our analysis shows that the guarantees on CTMC-based unmasking [ 17 ] have analogues for both fixed-cardinality unmasking [ 15 , 25 ] and Bernoulli unmasking. With this context, we now formally state the complexity relations: Proposition 3 (Connections between aggregate complexity measures) . For the full interval [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , the Bernoulli aggregate- UGC complexity is related to 𝖳𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{TSE} complexity via the relation 𝖧 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \displaystyle\mathsf{H}(0,1) = 2 d + 1 ​ 𝖳𝖲𝖤 ​ ( ℙ Z ) . \displaystyle=\frac{2}{d+1}\mathsf{TSE}(\mathbb{P}_{Z}). (62a) Moreover, the fixed-cardinality complexity 𝖧 card ​ ( 0 , d ) \mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{card}}(0,d) is sandwiched by the Bernoulli version 𝖧 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) ≤ 𝖧 card ​ ( 0 , d ) ≤ 2 ​ 𝖧 ​ ( 0 , 1 ) . \displaystyle\mathsf{H}(0,1)\;\leq\;\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{card}}(0,d)\;\leq\;2\mathsf{H}(0,1). (62b) Finally, the 𝖣𝖧𝖶 \mathsf{DHW} complexity satisfies the sandwich relation 𝖧 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) ≤ ( i ​ i ​ i ) 𝖣𝖧𝖶 ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) ≤ ( i ​ v ) e e − 1 ​ 𝖧 ​ ( 0 , 1 ) . \displaystyle\mathsf{H}(0,1)\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(iii)}}{{\leq}}\;\mathsf{DHW}(\mathbb{P}_{Z})\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(iv)}}{{\leq}}\;\frac{e}{e-1}\mathsf{H}(0,1). (62c) We prove these claims in Section C.1 ; let us highlight a few interesting features here. The proofs of both claims ( 62a ) and ( 62b ) make use of a Bernstein polynomial representation of 𝗁 \mathsf{h} , a result of independent interest. In particular, we show in Section B.2 that 𝗁 ⁡ ( t ) \displaystyle\mathsf{h}(t) = ∑ j = 0 d − 1 ( d − 1 j ) ​ t j ​ ( 1 − t ) d − 1 − j ​ 𝗁 j card , \displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\binom{d-1}{j}t^{j}(1-t)^{d-1-j}\mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j}, (63) so that 𝗁 \mathsf{h} is a polynomial of degree at most d − 1 d-1 . In proving the sandwich ( 62c ), we show that the 𝖣𝖧𝖶 \mathsf{DHW} complexity functional has the explicit representation 𝖣𝖧𝖶 ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) = ∫ 0 1 t ​ min ⁡ { 1 , log ⁡ ( 1 / t ) } ​ 𝗁 ′ ​ ( t ) ​ 𝑑 t \mathsf{DHW}(\mathbb{P}_{Z})=\int_{0}^{1}t\min\{1,\log(1/t)\}\mathsf{h}^{\prime}(t)dt , from which the estimates ( 62c ) follow from simple algebra. The analysis leading to this representation reveals an interesting algorithmic connection to Bernoulli unmasking: the DHW unmasking algorithm, while described and analyzed as a form of τ \tau -leaping [ 20 ] in a continuous-time Markov chain, is closely related to the Bernoulli unmasking sampler. See Section C.2 for details of this relation.

sections.heading: Appendix B Alternative representations of 𝗁 \mathsf{h}
sections.text: In this section, we develop and explore some alternative representations of 𝗁 \mathsf{h} and its derivative 𝗁 ′ \mathsf{h}^{\prime} that provide useful insight for subsequent proofs.

sections.heading: B.1 Proof of the identity ( 15a )
sections.text: In this appendix, we prove the random subset identity ( 15a ), namely that we can write 𝗁 ⁡ ( t ) = ∑ i = 1 d 𝔼 A i , t ​ [ Info ⁡ ( Z i ; Z A i , t ) ] , \displaystyle\mathsf{h}(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathbb{E}_{A_{i,t}}\big[\operatorname{Info}(Z_{i};Z_{A_{i,t}})\big], where A i , t ⊆ [ d ] ∖ { i } A_{i,t}\subseteq[d]\setminus\{i\} is a random subset obtained by including each coordinate of [ d ] ∖ { i } [d]\setminus\{i\} independently with probability t t . To prove this representation, for each i ∈ [ d ] i\in[d] , let E i E_{i} denote the event that coordinate i i remains masked at reveal time t t , and let A ≡ A i , t ⊆ [ d ] ∖ { i } A\equiv A_{i,t}\subseteq[d]\setminus\{i\} denote the set of revealed coordinates. Conditional on E i E_{i} , the observation X t X_{t} is equivalent to the pair ( A , Z A ) (A,Z_{A}) . Consequently, we have the mutual information identity Info ⁡ ( Z i ; X t ∣ E i ) = Info ⁡ ( Z i , A , Z A ) \operatorname{Info}(Z_{i};X_{t}\mid E_{i})=\operatorname{Info}\big(Z_{i};A,Z_{A}\big) . By the chain rule for mutual information, we have Info ⁡ ( Z i , A , Z A ) \displaystyle\operatorname{Info}\big(Z_{i};A,Z_{A}\big) = Info ⁡ ( Z i , A ) ⏟ = 0 + Info ⁡ ( Z i ; Z A ∣ A ) , \displaystyle=\underbrace{\operatorname{Info}(Z_{i};A)}_{=0}+\operatorname{Info}\big(Z_{i};Z_{A}\mid A\big), using the fact that Z i Z_{i} and A ≡ A i , t A\equiv A_{i,t} are independent. Conditioning on A = a A=a does not change the joint law of ( Z i , Z A ) (Z_{i},Z_{A}) , so that we have shown that Info ⁡ ( Z i ; X t ∣ E i ) = Info ⁡ ( Z i ; Z A ∣ A ) \displaystyle\operatorname{Info}(Z_{i};X_{t}\mid E_{i})\;=\;\operatorname{Info}(Z_{i};Z_{A}\mid A) = ∑ a ℙ ( A = a ) Info ( Z i ; Z a ) = 𝔼 A [ Info ( Z i ; Z A ) ] for each i = 1 , … , d . \displaystyle=\sum_{a}\mathbb{P}(A=a)\operatorname{Info}(Z_{i};Z_{a})=\mathbb{E}_{A}\big[\operatorname{Info}(Z_{i};Z_{A})\big]\qquad\mbox{for each $i=1,\ldots,d$.} Summing this identity over the coordinate index i i yields the claim ( 15a ).

sections.heading: B.2 Representation via Bernstein polynomials
sections.text: In this section, we develop representations of both 𝗁 \mathsf{h} and 𝗁 ′ \mathsf{h}^{\prime} as Bernstein polynomials in terms of the coefficients 𝗁 j card \mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j} . These representations have some useful immediate consequences, and are used in the proofs in Appendix C . Recall the definition of the coefficients 𝗁 j card \displaystyle\mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j} ≔ ∑ i = 1 d 𝔼 B i , j [ Info ( Z i ; Z B i , j ) ] where B i , j is uniform over j -cardinality subsets of [ d ] ∖ { i } . \displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathbb{E}_{B_{i,j}}\big[\operatorname{Info}(Z_{i};Z_{B_{i,j}})\big]\qquad\mbox{where $B_{i,j}$ is uniform over $j$-cardinality subsets of $[d]\setminus\{i\}$.} (64) Letting A i , t A_{i,t} be a Bernoulli random subset of [ d ] ∖ { i } [d]\setminus\{i\} with inclusion probability t t , we can write 𝗁 j card \displaystyle\mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j} = ∑ i = 1 d 𝔼 ⁡ [ Info ⁡ ( Z i ; Z A i , t ) ∣ card ⁡ ( A i , t ) = j ] . \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathbb{E}\Big[\operatorname{Info}(Z_{i};Z_{A_{i,t}})\mid\operatorname{card}(A_{i,t})=j\Big]. Since ℙ [ card ( A i , t ) = j ] = ( d − 1 j ) t j ( 1 − t ) d − 1 − j \mathbb{P}[\operatorname{card}(A_{i,t})=j]=\binom{d-1}{j}t^{j}(1-t)^{d-1-j} , it follows by combining the tower property with the representation ( 15a ) that 𝗁 ⁡ ( t ) \displaystyle\mathsf{h}(t) = ∑ j = 0 d − 1 ( d − 1 j ) ​ t j ​ ( 1 − t ) d − 1 − j ​ 𝗁 j card . \displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\binom{d-1}{j}t^{j}(1-t)^{d-1-j}\mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j}. (65a) Moreover, by differentiating equation ( 65a ), we obtain 𝗁 ′ ​ ( t ) \displaystyle\mathsf{h}^{\prime}(t) = ( d − 1 ) ​ ∑ j = 0 d − 2 ( d − 2 j ) ​ t j ​ ( 1 − t ) d − 2 − j ​ { 𝗁 j + 1 card − 𝗁 j card } . \displaystyle=(d-1)\sum_{j=0}^{d-2}\binom{d-2}{j}t^{j}(1-t)^{d-2-j}\big\{\mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j+1}-\mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j}\big\}. (65b) This calculation uses standard properties of derivatives of Bernstein polynomials [ 30 , 35 ] . (In particular, differentiation transforms coefficients into their first differences.) As one immediate consequence, from equation ( 65a ), we see that 𝗁 \mathsf{h} is a polynomial of degree at most d − 1 d-1 . It follows immediately that the derivative 𝗁 ′ \mathsf{h}^{\prime} exists. Let us develop two additional consequences.

sections.heading: B.2.1 Proof of 𝗁 \mathsf{h} -monotonicity
sections.text: We now prove that 𝗁 \mathsf{h} is monotone by showing that 𝗁 ′ ​ ( t ) ≥ 0 \mathsf{h}^{\prime}(t)\geq 0 . The Bernstein polynomial representation ( 65b ) of 𝗁 ′ \mathsf{h}^{\prime} shows that it suffices to prove that 𝗁 j + 1 card ≥ 𝗁 j card \mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j+1}\geq\mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j} . For 0 ≤ j ≤ d − 2 0\leq j\leq d-2 and a fixed coordinate i i , let A j A_{j} be a random subset, chosen uniformly from all the j j -element subsets of [ d ] ∖ { i } [d]\setminus\{i\} , and, conditionally on A j A_{j} , let J J be uniform over its complement inside [ d ] ∖ { i } [d]\setminus\{i\} . This defines a coupling between the subsets. Then the random set A j ∪ { J } A_{j}\cup\{J\} is uniform over the ( j + 1 ) (j+1) -element subsets, while the chain rule for mutual information gives the decomposition Info ⁡ ( Z i ; Z A j ∪ { J } ) − Info ⁡ ( Z i ; Z A j ) = Info ⁡ ( Z i ; Z J ∣ Z A j ) ≥ 0 \operatorname{Info}(Z_{i};Z_{A_{j}\cup\{J\}})-\operatorname{Info}(Z_{i};Z_{A_{j}})=\operatorname{Info}(Z_{i};Z_{J}\mid Z_{A_{j}})\geq 0 . Averaging first over the coupling and then over i i shows that 𝗁 j + 1 card − 𝗁 j card ≥ 0 \mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j+1}-\mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j}\geq 0 , as claimed.

sections.heading: B.2.2 Proof of the total-correlation representations ( 61b )
sections.text: Now let us prove the representations of the total correlation 𝖳𝖢 \mathsf{TC} and dual total correlation 𝖣𝖳𝖢 \mathsf{DTC} given in equation ( 61b ). From the random subset representation ( 15a ) of 𝗁 \mathsf{h} , we have 𝗁 ⁡ ( 1 ) \displaystyle\mathsf{h}(1) = ∑ i = 1 d Info ⁡ ( Z i ; Z − i ) = ∑ i = 1 d { Ent ⁡ ( Z i ) − Ent ⁡ ( Z i ∣ Z − i ) } , \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\operatorname{Info}(Z_{i};Z_{-i})\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{d}\big\{\operatorname{Ent}(Z_{i})-\operatorname{Ent}(Z_{i}\mid Z_{-i})\big\}, where the second equality expands the definition of mutual information. By comparing with the definitions ( 61a ), we see immediately that 𝗁 ⁡ ( 1 ) = 𝖳𝖢 ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) + 𝖣𝖳𝖢 ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) \mathsf{h}(1)=\mathsf{TC}(\mathbb{P}_{Z})+\mathsf{DTC}(\mathbb{P}_{Z}) . Since 𝗁 ⁡ ( 1 ) = ∫ 0 1 𝗁 ′ ​ ( t ) ​ 𝑑 t \mathsf{h}(1)=\int_{0}^{1}\mathsf{h}^{\prime}(t)dt , using the fact that 𝗁 ⁡ ( 0 ) = 0 \mathsf{h}(0)=0 , if we can prove the identity 𝖳𝖢 ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) = ∫ 0 1 ( 1 − t ) ​ 𝗁 ′ ​ ( t ) ​ 𝑑 t \mathsf{TC}(\mathbb{P}_{Z})=\int_{0}^{1}(1-t)\mathsf{h}^{\prime}(t)dt , then it follows that 𝖣𝖳𝖢 ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) = ∫ 0 1 t ​ 𝗁 ′ ​ ( t ) ​ 𝑑 t \mathsf{DTC}(\mathbb{P}_{Z})=\int_{0}^{1}t\mathsf{h}^{\prime}(t)dt . Accordingly, the remainder of our analysis focuses on the 𝖳𝖢 \mathsf{TC} representation. For j = 1 , … , d j=1,\ldots,d , let e j e_{j} be the entropy coefficient defined in equation ( 60 ), along with e 0 = 0 e_{0}=0 . Note that we have e 1 = 1 d ​ ∑ i = 1 d Ent ⁡ ( Z i ) e_{1}=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\operatorname{Ent}(Z_{i}) , and e d = Ent ⁡ ( Z ) e_{d}=\operatorname{Ent}(Z) . For any i ∈ [ d ] i\in[d] and A ⊆ [ d ] ∖ { i } A\subseteq[d]\setminus\{i\} , we have the mutual information identity Info ⁡ ( Z i ; Z A ) = Ent ⁡ ( Z i ) + Ent ⁡ ( Z A ) − Ent ⁡ ( Z A ∪ { i } ) \operatorname{Info}(Z_{i};Z_{A})=\operatorname{Ent}(Z_{i})+\operatorname{Ent}(Z_{A})-\operatorname{Ent}(Z_{A\cup\{i\}}) . It can be averaged over i i and over uniform j j -cardinality subsets A A . Doing so and using the definition ( 15b ) of the 𝗁 j card \mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j} coefficients, we find that 𝗁 j card = d ⁡ ( e 1 + e j − e j + 1 ) . \displaystyle\mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j}=d\big(e_{1}+e_{j}-e_{j+1}\big). (66) Substituting this identity into the Bernstein representation ( 65a ) and integrating over the interval [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] yields ∫ 0 1 𝗁 ⁡ ( t ) ​ 𝑑 t \displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\mathsf{h}(t)\,dt = ∑ j = 0 d − 1 ( d − 1 j ) ​ 𝗁 j card ​ { ∫ 0 1 t j ​ ( 1 − t ) d − 1 − j ​ 𝑑 t } = ( i ) 1 d ​ ∑ j = 0 d − 1 𝗁 j card = ( i ​ i ) d ​ e 1 − e d = ( i ​ i ​ i ) 𝖳𝖢 ⁡ ( ℙ Z ) , \displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\binom{d-1}{j}\mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j}\big\{\int_{0}^{1}t^{j}(1-t)^{d-1-j}dt\}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(i)}}{{=}}\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(ii)}}{{=}}de_{1}-e_{d}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(iii)}}{{=}}\mathsf{TC}(\mathbb{P}_{Z}), where step (i) uses the beta-integral identity ∫ 0 1 ( d − 1 j ) ​ t j ​ ( 1 − t ) d − 1 − j ​ 𝑑 t = 1 d \int_{0}^{1}\binom{d-1}{j}t^{j}(1-t)^{d-1-j}\,dt=\frac{1}{d} ; step (ii) uses the identity ( 66 ) along with some algebra; and step (iii) follows from the definition ( 61a ) of the total correlation, combined with the definition ( 60 ) of the entropy coefficients. sections.heading: Appendix C Proofs of connecting results
sections.text: In this section, we prove various results that connect the UGC aggregate complexity to other complexity notions ( Section C.1 ), and compare the DHW τ \tau -leaping unmasking algorithm with the Bernoulli unmasking procedure ( Section C.2 ).

sections.heading: C.1 Proof of Proposition 3
sections.text: The proposition consists of three claims, and we prove each of them in turn.

sections.heading: C.1.1 Proof of 𝖳𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{TSE} identity ( 62a )
sections.text: Beginning with the definition ( 2c ), integration by parts yields 𝖧 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) = ∫ 0 1 ( 2 ​ t − 1 ) ​ 𝗁 ​ ( t ) ​ 𝑑 t \mathsf{H}(0,1)=\int_{0}^{1}(2t-1)\mathsf{h}(t)\,dt , where the boundary term vanishes since t ⁡ ( 1 − t ) = 0 t(1-t)=0 at the endpoints. Substituting the Bernstein representation ( 65a ) of 𝗁 \mathsf{h} into this equation yields 𝖧 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \displaystyle\mathsf{H}(0,1) = ∑ j = 0 d − 1 𝗁 j card ​ ( d − 1 j ) ​ { ∫ 0 1 ( 2 ​ t − 1 ) ​ t j ​ ( 1 − t ) d − 1 − j ​ 𝑑 t } = 1 d ⁡ ( d + 1 ) ​ ∑ j = 0 d − 1 ( 2 ​ j − d + 1 ) ​ 𝗁 j card , \displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j}\binom{d-1}{j}\left\{\int_{0}^{1}(2t-1)t^{j}(1-t)^{d-1-j}dt\right\}\;=\;\frac{1}{d(d+1)}\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}(2j-d+1)\;\mathsf{h}^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\operatorname{card}}}_{j}, (67) where the second step follows from a standard beta-integral identity. Wainwright mjwain@mit.edu Lab for Information and Decision Systems Statistics and Data Science Center EECS and Mathematics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology August 24, 2026 Abstract We study masking diffusion for discrete sampling and introduce a path-resolved measure of data geometry called the unmasking growth complexity ( UGC ). Its local increments directly control Kullback–Leibler (KL) discretization error, yielding a unified analysis of Bernoulli-subset and fixed-cardinality unmasking schemes. In log-reveal-odds coordinates, this structure yields optimized single-block and multi-block schedules, and quantifies the gains from adapting computational effort to data geometry. Crucially, we show how UGC increments can be estimated from samples via KL increments along coupled reveal trajectories. This leads to certified-optimal samplers that achieve a prescribed KL error with high probability and iteration complexity within a constant factor of the corresponding oracle procedure. Collapsing the UGC path yields the aggregate UGC mass, which connects to classical multivariate dependence measures, and complexity measures from previous analyses of discrete diffusion. In the fine-partition limit, the squared integral of the square-root UGC density determines the sharp leading-order optimal Euler discretization error. Examples exhibit substantial dimension-dependent gains over coarse schedules, including Ω ~ ​ ( d ) \widetilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{d}) improvements achievable with a constant number of adaptively placed blocks. 1 Introduction The problem of sampling from a high-dimensional distribution is fundamental in nature, and has a wide range of applications. Efficient sampling algorithms underpin the utility of Monte Carlo approximation [ 39 , 42 ] ; support uncertainty quantification in Bayesian models [ 18 , 6 ] ; and lie at the heart of generative AI [ 40 , 16 , 54 , 13 ] . Recent years have witnessed tremendous practical and theoretical advances in the use of diffusion 1 1 1 In full generality, the diffusion terminology is a misnomer, since not all such models involve a diffusion process in the formal probabilistic sense; this includes the unmasking models studied in this paper. Nonetheless, we adopt the conventional terminology. sampling algorithms, which generate samples via a sequence of “denoising” operations [ 45 , 46 , 23 , 47 , 14 , 12 , 5 ] . Initial work in the area focused on sampling from continuous distributions in d , in which case the denoising step corresponds to estimating a signal embedded in Gaussian noise [ 23 , 47 ] . A more recent line of work, and the general focus of this paper, has focused on sampling from discrete distributions, using various kinds of denoising processes [ 24 , 3 , 9 , 31 , 44 , 43 , 15 , 17 ] . In this paper, we study the problem of sampling a random vector Z ∈ ( 𝒜 ) d Z\in(\mathcal{A})^{d} , where 𝒜 \mathcal{A} is a discrete alphabet, and d d is the ambient dimension. While various samplers have been devised, we focus on unmasking samplers , which traverse a path from a fully unobserved vector, denoted by Z ∗ = ( ⋆ , … , ⋆ ) Z^{*}=(\star,\ldots,\star) with ⋆ \star meaning masked or unobserved, back to a sample Z ∼ ℙ Z Z\sim\mathbb{P}_{Z} from the target distribution. The path is traversed via a sequence of unmasking operations, in which a subset of the masked coordinates are revealed. Unmasking algorithms differ in the form and sequence by which these unmasking steps take place. Unmasking and closely related mask-based generative samplers have proven effective across a range of applications, including machine translation [ 19 ] , image and video synthesis [ 11 , 55 ] , text-to-image generation [ 10 ] , speech synthesis [ 52 ] , language modeling [ 43 , 33 ] , and protein design [ 51 ] . 1.1 Overview This paper is motivated by two broad questions associated with diffusion samplers, as articulated in our companion paper on Gaussian diffusion [ 50 ] , which we paraphrase here: Q1: Can the performance of masked diffusion sampling be explained and quantified, in some generality, by a measure tied to data geometry? Q2: Is it possible to exploit a masked-diffusion measure of data geometry to design, optimize and certify practical sampling schemes? Recent work has made substantial progress on both questions. Chen et al. [ 15 ] analyze fixed-cardinality unmasking and derive an exact information-profile representation of its expected KL discretization error, with consequences for schedule design and bounds based on total and dual total correlation. Lavenant and Zanella [ 25 ] derive an information-profile representation of the factorization error for random-order unmasking, and study optimal schedules in asymptotic scaling regimes. From a different direction, Dmitriev et al. [ 17 ] analyze discrete diffusion via a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) formulation; for masking diffusion, their modified τ \tau -leaping guarantees are governed by an effective total correlation that can be substantially smaller than the classical worst-case measures. Collectively, these results provide important answers to Q1 and partial answers to Q2 , but fall short of finite-sample guarantees for learning and certifying geometry-adaptive schedules from data. Our answer to Q1 is based on the unmasking growth complexity or UGC for short. It is a path-resolved measure of data dependence along the reveal process. We show that its local increments directly control KL discretization error, thereby obtaining a common analysis of both fixed-cardinality unmasking and a natural Bernoulli-subset variant. When collapsed over the full reveal path, the UGC complexity reduces to a coarse measure that closely connected to classical multivariate dependence measures [ 53 , 21 , 22 , 48 ] , as well as to the effective total correlation appearing in the CTMC analysis [ 17 ] . Consequently, the resulting single-block guarantees sharpen existing fixed-cardinality bounds while giving Bernoulli unmasking guarantees comparable to those available for CTMC samplers. The main contributions of our paper are in the context of Q2 , and in particular, our use of the full UGC complexity path to design and analyze sampling algorithms that are certified-optimal. More precisely, we show that UGC complexity has a natural additive structure along the reveal path, so that its local increments can be estimated from samples and used to allocate computational effort where the target distribution is most difficult to unmask. We exploit this structure to derive and optimize blockwise schedules, construct data-dependent samplers with high-probability KL certificates, and finally, to optimize the block boundaries themselves. In the fine-partition limit, the log-reveal-odds UGC density emerges as the intrinsic local geometry: its square-root integral governs the limiting partition complexity and the sharp leading-order optimal Euler discretization error. 1.2 Related work So as to put our results in context, we now provide a broader discussion of related work. There are various types of discrete diffusion models, all of which replace the additive Gaussian noise for continuous-space diffusions by stochastic corruption kernels on discrete state spaces. Early work developed multinomial and more general structured discrete diffusion processes [ 24 , 3 ] , among them the absorbing-state corruption that underlies a masking diffusion process. Other work [ 9 ] formulated discrete diffusion models using the formalism of continuous-time Markov chains, with subsequent work developing discrete analogues of score-based modeling in which the reverse CTMC is parameterized through learned probability ratios [ 31 ] . Masked diffusion is a particularly important subclass, in which coordinates are corrupted by replacement with a distinguished mask symbol and generation proceeds by progressively reconstructing masked coordinates [ 44 , 43 ] . As described above, recent work has made progress on characterizing the accuracy–parallelism trade-off in random-order unmasking with fixed-cardinality subsets. In particular, Li and Cai [ 26 ] established information-theoretic convergence guarantees for parallel masked-diffusion sampling. Chen et al. [ 15 ] derived an exact characterization of the expected KL divergence in terms of a one-dimensional information profile; they also gave explicit sampling guarantees involving classical multivariate dependence measures [ 53 , 21 , 22 ] , namely the total correlation ( 𝖳𝖢 \mathsf{TC} ) and dual total correlation ( 𝖣𝖳𝖢 \mathsf{DTC} ). A portion of our analysis exploits their exact KL representation. Lavenant and Zanella [ 25 ] derived an information-profile representation for the factorization error of random-order unmasking, and then studied optimal scheduling via a continuum scaling limit. We compare their asymptotic schedule analysis more closely with our fine-partition and Euler results following Theorem 3 . The τ \tau -leaping method for continuous-time Markov chains (CTMC) originates in stochastic chemical kinetics, where its consistency and approximation errors have been studied extensively [ 20 , 36 , 27 , 2 ] . For discrete diffusion, recent work has developed convergence guarantees for τ \tau -leaping under both standard and absorbing corruption processes [ 37 , 28 , 29 , 17 ] , as well as higher-order variants of CTMC discretization [ 38 ] . Among CTMC analyses, most related to our work is the paper of Dmitriev et al. [ 17 ] , who analyze a modified τ \tau -leaping sampler for a general class of CTMC discrete diffusion models. For masking diffusion, they give guarantees in terms of a measure that they call effective total correlation, which turns out to be closely related to the coarse UGC complexity that we introduce. In contrast to CTMC-based analyses, we study Bernoulli and fixed-cardinality unmasking; our coarse UGC bounds yield matching guarantees for these direct schemes. The coarse UGC complexity is also connected to several multivariate dependence measures, including 𝖳𝖢 \mathsf{TC} , 𝖣𝖳𝖢 \mathsf{DTC} , and the finer-grained measure of Tononi et al. [ 48 ] . We develop these connections in Appendix A . Finally, in our companion paper [ 50 ] on Gaussian diffusion sampling, we introduced the denoising growth complexity ( DGC ), a pathwise complexity that controls KL discretization error, and whose log-scale DGC density specifies optimal sampling schedules. Despite the substantial differences between Gaussian and masking diffusion, the two theories exhibit a remarkable degree of parallelism, suggesting a common underlying principle linking denoising growth, KL discretization error, and optimal scheduling. 2 Overview: unmasking growth complexity and sampling So as to orient the reader, we begin by providing a high-level overview of the main ideas and quantities underlying our analysis. We first describe the canonical unmasking process. Using it, we define the unmasking growth complexity ( UGC ), which measures how informational difficulty is distributed along the reveal path. We then pass to log-reveal-odds coordinates, where this complexity is represented by a density whose geometry determines how sampling effort should be allocated along the path. Our goal here is primarily conceptual: to explain the distinction between coarse and geometry-aware schedules, to illustrate the data geometry of the UGC density on several examples, and to preview how data-driven adaptive partitioning can exploit this geometry. Precise forms of our guarantees for samplers, estimation procedures, and supporting technical results are developed in the subsequent sections. 2.1 Unmasking reveal process Given a discrete alphabet 𝒜 \mathcal{A} , our goal is to sample a d d -dimensional random vector Z ∈ 𝒜 d Z\in\mathcal{A}^{d} with distribution ℙ Z \mathbb{P}_{Z} . At a high level, they involve two basic operations: choosing a subset of indices and then, conditional on this subset, making a random choice of values for the revealed variables using the denoiser μ \mu . The samplers that we analyze differ only in how the random subset is chosen: the Bernoulli sampler uses coin flips, thereby generating a set with a random cardinality, whereas the fixed-cardinality sampler chooses a random subset with fixed cardinality.
